root.label: Aldabra giant tortoise survey finds 180,000 tortoises

events.label: Aldabra giant tortoise survey finds 180,000 tortoises

slots.name: population estimate
slots.sentence: Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

slots.name: adult population estimate
slots.sentence: The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

slots.name: historic population estimate
slots.sentence: It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

slots.name: historical low count
slots.sentence: In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.

slots.name: wild locations
slots.sentence: Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.

slots.name: survey duration
slots.sentence: The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022.

slots.name: invasive mammal types
slots.sentence: The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings.
